paragraphs.text: A piece is free when it is attacked and nobody defends it. Taking it costs you nothing. Most games between beginners are decided by free pieces, so spotting them is the first habit worth building.
The habit: checks, captures, threats
Before every move, look at the board in this order:
1. Checks. Can either side give check?
2. Captures. Every capture you could make, and every capture your opponent could make.
3. Threats. What does your opponent's last move attack?
It takes a few seconds and catches most free pieces, yours and your opponent's.
Is it really free? Count
A piece that is attacked is not always free. Count attackers and defenders. If the piece is defended, taking it usually means losing your own piece back.

When a piece is attacked twice and defended once, the second attacker usually wins it. Capture with your least valuable piece first, so that if the opponent recaptures, you lose as little as possible.
Now you
The first puzzles come with a hint. After that you are on your own, and in the final set nobody tells you what to look for.

examples.answer_text: The black knight on d5 is attacked by the rook and defended by nothing. Rxd5 wins a whole knight for free.
Same idea, one difference: the pawn on e6 defends the knight. Rxd5? exd5 and White has traded a rook (5) for a knight (3). Count before you capture.

paragraphs.text: Checkmate ends the game: the king is in check, and there is no way out. There are only three ways out of a check, and a mate takes all three away:
1. Move the king to a safe square.
2. Block the check by putting a piece in between.
3. Capture the piece that gives check.
To find a mate in one, look at every check you can give, and for each one ask the three questions.
Mating with help
A queen next to the enemy king is mate if it can't be captured, so it needs a defender. Often that defender is your own king.
The habit
When the enemy king has few free squares, especially stuck behind its own pawns, start your search with checks. The forcing moves come first.

examples.answer_text: The back-rank mate. Ra8+ attacks the king along the 8th rank. The king can't move, because its own pawns block f7, g7 and h7. Nothing can block or capture the rook: mate.
Qg7# The queen gives check from g7. The black king can't take it, because the white king on g6 defends it, and every flight square (g8, h7) is covered too.

paragraphs.text: A fork is one piece attacking two (or more) enemy pieces at once. Your opponent can only save one of them, so you win the other.
Every piece can fork, but the knight is the champion: it jumps, it attacks in eight directions, and the pieces it attacks can never attack it back.
Pawn forks
Pawns fork too, and because a pawn is worth so little, any fork it makes wins material.
How to look for forks

Look for two enemy pieces that are undefended or more valuable than your attacking piece, especially the king and queen. Then ask: is there a square from which one of my pieces attacks both? Check whether that square is safe.

examples.answer_text: Nc7+ attacks the king and the rook on a8 at the same time. The king must move, and then the knight takes the rook. A check plus an attack on something valuable is the strongest kind of fork.
d5 attacks the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6 at once. Black can save only one of them.

paragraphs.text: A pin freezes a piece: it stands on a line between an attacker and something more valuable behind it. If it moves, the piece behind is exposed.
• Absolute pin: the piece behind is the king. The pinned piece is not allowed to move at all.
• Relative pin: the piece behind is valuable (often the queen). Moving is legal, but it loses material.
Only long-range pieces pin: bishops, rooks and queens.
Pile up on the pinned piece
A pinned piece can't escape, so you can attack it with more pieces than it has defenders.
How to look for pins
Line up the enemy king or queen with your bishops, rooks and queen. Is there exactly one piece in between? Then ask what that piece is defending, and how you can attack it again.

examples.answer_text: Bb5 pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8: the knight may not move. Then d5 attacks it with a pawn, and the knight can neither run nor be defended in time. A pinned piece is a target: attack it again.

The knight on d5 is pinned to the queen on d8 by the rook on d1, and attacked twice (bishop and rook) while defended once. Bxd5 Qxd5 Rxd5: White wins a knight. Count attackers and defenders, then capture.

paragraphs.text: A skewer is a pin turned inside out. The more valuable piece stands in front, the less valuable one behind it on the same line. You attack the front piece, it has to move, and you take the one behind.
Skewers are strongest with a check: the king must step out of the line, and whatever stood behind it falls.
How to look for skewers

Look for two enemy pieces on the same rank, file or diagonal, with the more valuable one (king, queen, rook) in front and nothing in between. If one of your long-range pieces can reach that line, preferably with check, you have a skewer.

examples.answer_text: Rd1+ checks the king on d5 along the d-file. The king must leave the file, and the rook takes the queen that was hiding behind it on d8.

paragraphs.text: In a discovered attack, one piece moves out of the way and uncovers an attack by a piece standing behind it. Two pieces attack at once: the one that moved, and the one revealed.
When the uncovered attack is a check, it's a discovered check. The opponent must answer the check, so the piece that moved is free to grab almost anything.
How to look for discovered attacks

Look for your own piece standing between one of your long-range pieces (bishop, rook, queen) and an enemy target, especially the king. Then ask: where can the piece in front go to do damage of its own? A capture, a check, or an attack on the queen makes the discovery decisive.

examples.answer_text: The knight blocks the rook's line to the black king. Nxc5+ takes the queen and uncovers the rook's check along the e-file at the same time. Black must deal with the check and can't recapture.

paragraphs.text: A mate in two is a forcing sequence: your first move leaves the opponent no good answer, and your second move is mate. The first move is usually a check or a sacrifice that drives the king where you want it.
Work backwards: picture the mating position first, then find a forcing move that gets you there.
The habit
In every mate in two, check the forcing moves first: checks, then captures, then threats. After each candidate, list every reply the opponent has. If each one leaves you a mate, you've found it.

examples.answer_text: The rook ladder. Rb7+ drives the king to the 8th rank (the 6th is covered by the rook on a6). Then Ra8# : one rook covers the 7th rank, the other gives check on the 8th. The rooks take turns.
